title: The History of Branding: From Cattle Marks to AI
description: The complete history of branding, from ownership marks on livestock and trade goods 4,000 years ago to trademarks, brand management, corporate identity, positioning, brand equity, social media and AI, and what it teaches anyone building a brand today.
body:
The history of branding is the story of how a burn mark on a cow became the most valuable asset a company owns.

Branding is the practice of giving a product, service or organization a distinct identity (a name, a mark, a look, a voice and a promise) so people can recognize it, tell it apart from the alternatives and decide whether to trust it.

That practice is more than 4,000 years old, and it did not start with logos or advertising.

It started with fire.

I have spent nearly 20 years designing brand identities, and the longer I do it, the more I notice that every era of branding added a new job for a brand to do, and none of the old jobs ever went away.

Here are the key takeaways.

  • Origin: the word brand comes from the Old English and Old Norse words for fire, and the oldest brands were marks of ownership on livestock and trade goods.
  • Ancient makers: potters, lamp makers and merchants in the Indus Valley, Rome and China marked goods to signal origin and quality long before trademarks existed.
  • Modern branding: mass production, packaging and trademark law in the 1800s turned marks into legal property and household names.
  • Brand management: a 1931 memo at Procter & Gamble made the brand something a person is responsible for running.
  • Meaning over marks: from the 1950s onward, corporate identity, positioning, brand equity and emotional branding moved the brand from the package into the customer’s mind.
  • Today: social media and AI made everyone a publisher, so a brand is now shaped as much by its audience as by its owner.

What is branding?

Branding is the ongoing work of shaping how people recognize, understand and feel about a company, product or person.

The definitions get mixed up, so here is how I separate the terms.

  • Brand: the perception people hold: what they expect from you and what they tell other people about you (see what is a brand).
  • Branding: the deliberate actions that shape that perception: strategy, naming, design, messaging and behavior.
  • Brand identity: the tangible system people see and hear: logo, color, typography, imagery and voice (see branding vs. brand identity).
  • Marketing: the campaigns and channels that put the brand in front of buyers.

Marty Neumeier’s definition from The Brand Gap is the one most designers use today: a brand is a person’s gut feeling about a product, service or organization.

When I interviewed him for my podcast, he called “a brand is a logo” the oldest wrong definition out there, and stressed that it is the customer’s gut feeling that counts, never the company’s.

It took about four millennia to get from a burn mark to a gut feeling.

If you want the definition argued from ten angles, I collected them in what is branding, defined by 10 experts.

The rest of this guide explains how we got here.

History of branding timeline

Here is the whole history of branding in one table, with the job that each era added to the brand.

EraWhat a brand didExamples

Each row gets its own section below.

Where does the word “brand” come from?

The word brand comes from the Old English brand (also spelled brond), meaning fire, flame or torch, from the same Germanic root as the Old Norse brandr.

Poets also used it for a sword, because a blade flashes like flame, and brand-new originally meant fresh from the fire.

According to the Online Etymology Dictionary, the verb meaning to burn a mark with a hot iron dates from around 1400, and the noun for the mark itself, notably on casks, from the 1550s.

That covered cattle, timber and barrels, and also people: criminals, vagrants and enslaved people were branded too, which is why the word still carries a second meaning of stigma.

The commercial sense arrived late.

Brand meaning a particular make of goods is first recorded in 1854, after producers had spent decades burning their marks into crates and barrels of wine, tobacco and ale.

Brand name follows in 1889 and brand loyalty only in 1961.

So the vocabulary of branding is young, even though the practice is ancient.

Ancient branding: ownership and origin (before 500 CE)

The first brands answered one question: whose is this?

Livestock branding in ancient Egypt

Egyptian tomb art shows herdsmen throwing cattle to the ground and pressing hot irons into their hides while a scribe records the count.

The clearest scenes date from the New Kingdom, around 3,400 years ago, such as the tomb of Nebamun recorded by the Metropolitan Museum, and Egyptologists trace the practice back further, to the Old Kingdom.

You will often see 2700 BCE quoted as the date of the first branded cattle; I could not find an Egyptological source for that figure, so I am sticking to the evidence that exists.

A brand could not be washed off, lost or argued with, which made it the ideal proof of ownership for an asset that wanders.

Ranchers still brand cattle the same way, so the oldest branding technology in the world has never gone out of use.

Seals in the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia

Merchants of the Indus Valley civilization pressed carved stone seals into clay tags tied to bundles of trade goods between roughly 2600 and 1900 BCE.

Those seals, with their animal motifs and short inscriptions, have been found as far away as Mesopotamia and Central Asia, which means a mark made in one city was read and trusted in another.

Business historians Karl Moore and Susan Reid argue in their paper The Birth of Brand: 4000 Years of Branding that these marks already carried the two kinds of information a brand carries now: where a product came from and how good it was.

Status, added value and personality, they argue, were layered on top much later.

Makers’ marks in Greece and Rome

Greek potters signed their vases, and Roman workshops stamped bricks, roof tiles and the handles of the amphorae that carried wine and olive oil across the empire.

The best-known Roman brand is FORTIS, a name pressed into the base of mass-produced clay oil lamps made in northern Italy from about 70 to 230 CE.

FORTIS lamps sold across the empire, and provincial workshops copied the stamp for generations.

A counterfeit only makes sense when the mark itself is worth something, so FORTIS is arguably the earliest evidence of brand value.

In Pompeii, the fish-sauce magnate Aulus Umbricius Scaurus decorated the atrium of his house with a mosaic of four jars labeled with his own products, three of them carrying his name.

His labeled jars have been found around the Mediterranean: a product name, a quality claim and a named maker, on packaging, in the first century.

The White Rabbit of Song-dynasty China

China’s Northern Song dynasty (960–1127) had paper, printing and a booming urban consumer economy, and it produced what the National Museum of China calls the earliest known trademark advertisement.

It is a small bronze printing plate for Jinan Liu’s Fine Needle Shop.

The plate carries the shop’s name, a white rabbit pounding medicine as the shop’s symbol, an instruction to recognize the white rabbit at the door as the mark, and a line of copy about fine needles made from quality steel.

Name, logo, tagline and a call to action on one flyer, around a thousand years ago.

Medieval branding: guilds and hallmarks (500–1700)

In medieval Europe a mark stopped being optional and became an obligation.

The guilds that controlled each craft required members to mark their work so that poor quality could be traced back to the person who made it.

  • Bakers: England’s Assize of Bread and Ale, traditionally dated 1266, fixed the weight and price of a loaf, and is often cited, including by WIPO, as obliging bakers to mark their bread so a short-weight loaf could be traced.
  • Goldsmiths: a 1300 statute of Edward I required silver to be tested and struck with a leopard’s head, a 1363 ordinance added the maker’s own mark, and from 1478 pieces were assayed at Goldsmiths’ Hall in London, the likely origin of the word hallmark.
  • Papermakers: mills in Fabriano, Italy, began working watermarks into their sheets in 1282.
  • Printers: Johann Fust and Peter Schoeffer put the first printer’s mark in the Mainz Psalter of 1457, and Aldus Manutius of Venice adopted his dolphin and anchor in 1502.
  • Merchants: personal merchants’ marks were painted on bales and barrels so cargo could be identified after a shipwreck or a theft.

The hallmark is the important one for the history of branding.

It was a mark of quality backed by an independent authority rather than by the seller, which makes it the ancestor of every certification badge from Fairtrade to USDA Organic.

Two other medieval habits shaped how brands look.

Heraldry taught Europe to read simple shapes and flat colors as identity at a distance, and its logic survives in the crests of Porsche, Alfa Romeo and most football clubs.

Shop and inn signs did the same job in the street for customers who could not read: a boot for the cobbler, three golden balls for the pawnbroker, a red lion for the pub.

Some medieval names are still trading, although the dates on the labels deserve a second look.

Stella Artois prints 1366 on every bottle, the year of a tax record for the Den Hoorn brewery in Leuven, but the Artois family arrived in 1717 and the Stella brand launched in 1926.

Beretta holds up better: a 1526 invoice to the Republic of Venice for 185 gun barrels survives in the Venetian state archives, and the family still runs the company.

Heritage is a brand asset, and brands have been polishing it for a long time.

The Industrial Revolution and packaged goods (1750–1900)

Modern branding was invented to solve a problem that factories created.

Before industrialization you bought soap, flour or biscuits by weight from a shopkeeper you knew, scooped from an unmarked barrel.

The shopkeeper was the brand.

Factories, railways and cheap printed packaging changed that: a manufacturer could now sell identical goods to millions of strangers hundreds of miles away.

The package had to do the work the shopkeeper used to do: introduce the product, vouch for it and make it easy to ask for by name.

Harvard Business School historian Nancy Koehn makes the same point in her study of brand builders from Wedgwood to Dell: brands emerge in periods of upheaval, when sellers must win the trust of distant, anonymous buyers.

Josiah Wedgwood, the first modern brand builder

The English potter Josiah Wedgwood worked most of it out a century before the packaged-goods boom.

He founded his pottery in 1759 and impressed his own name into the base of his wares at a time when notable potters did not.

In the 1760s he won the patronage of Queen Charlotte, renamed his cream-colored earthenware Queen’s Ware and styled himself Potter to Her Majesty.

He opened a London showroom, printed illustrated catalogs, sent out travelling salesmen and offered a money-back guarantee.

Celebrity endorsement, premium positioning and direct marketing, in the 1770s.

Soap, oats and soda

The late 1800s produced names that are still on shelves.

  • Pears: Thomas Barratt signed the actress Lillie Langtry as an endorser in 1882 and bought the Millais painting Bubbles in 1886 to turn fine art into soap advertising.
  • Quaker Oats (1877): registered a man in Quaker dress as the first trademark for a breakfast cereal, borrowing the Quakers’ reputation for honesty.
  • Ivory (1879): Procter & Gamble sold a plain white soap on two claims, 99 and 44/100 percent pure (1882) and It Floats (1891).
  • Coca-Cola (1886): bookkeeper Frank Mason Robinson named the drink and wrote the logo in Spencerian script, the standard business handwriting of the day.
  • Heinz (1896): Henry Heinz adopted 57 Varieties as a slogan even though the company already made more than that.
  • Campbell’s (1898): adopted a red and white label after an executive admired Cornell University’s football uniforms.
  • Uneeda Biscuit (1898–99): the National Biscuit Company and the N.W. Ayer agency launched a sealed, moisture-proof package with what is often described as the first million-dollar advertising campaign.

Notice how many of those brands have a face.

The Quaker man, the Michelin Man (1898) and the Morton Salt girl (1914) gave a distant factory a human stand-in for the shopkeeper it had replaced, and the tradition of brand mascots has never stopped.

Packaging became a brand asset in its own right in 1915, when Coca-Cola briefed glassmakers for a bottle so distinctive that you could recognize it by feel in the dark, or lying broken on the ground.

The Root Glass Company’s contour bottle, patented that November, was the answer, and it is still one of the most recognized shapes on earth.

How trademark law made brands property (1857–1946)

A brand worth copying needs a law against copying it.

For most of history a maker whose mark was forged had little recourse beyond the guild or a fraud claim.

The nineteenth century fixed that within a few decades.

  • 1857: France passed the first comprehensive trademark registration law.
  • 1862: Britain’s Merchandise Marks Act made it a crime to imitate another trader’s mark with intent to defraud.
  • 1870: the first US federal trademark law; the Supreme Court struck it down in 1879, and narrower acts followed in 1881 and 1905.
  • 1875: Britain’s Trade Marks Registration Act created a national register, which opened on January 1, 1876.
  • 1883 and 1891: the Paris Convention and the Madrid Agreement began protecting marks across borders.
  • 1946: the Lanham Act created the modern US trademark system, which is still in force.

The first entry in the British register is the Bass & Co. pale ale label with its red triangle, UK trade mark number 1, and it is still in force today.

Brewery legend says a Bass employee spent New Year’s Eve queuing outside the registrar’s office to be first through the door; the UK Intellectual Property Office, which tells the story itself, is careful to say “reportedly”.

The triangle was already famous enough that Édouard Manet painted two bottles of Bass on the counter of A Bar at the Folies-Bergère in 1882, which makes it a contender for the first product placement in a masterpiece.

In the United States, the first federal registration went to the Averill Chemical Paint Company for an eagle in October 1870, and the oldest US mark still in use is Samson’s rope trademark of a man wrestling a lion, registered in 1884.

Registration changed what a brand was.

A mark was now an asset that could be owned, defended, licensed and sold separately from the factory that made the goods, and every later idea about brand value rests on that.

If you are at this stage yourself, I cover the practical side in how to trademark a logo and in a podcast conversation with trademark attorney Andrei Mincov on how to trademark your brand.

The advertising age: agencies, radio and TV (1840s–1950)

Once brands were property, an industry grew up to make them famous.

Volney Palmer set up as America’s first advertising agent in Philadelphia in the early 1840s, selling newspaper space on commission.

N.W. Ayer & Son (1869) and J. Walter Thompson, who bought the New York agency he worked for in 1877, turned the space broker into the full-service agency that wrote the ads, planned the campaigns and researched the buyers.

Around 1900 Thompson’s house publications were urging manufacturers to invest in trademark advertising, which is what we now call brand advertising.

Claude Hopkins’s 1923 book Scientific Advertising argued that ads should be tested and measured like any other investment, with coupons doing the job analytics does today.

Then mass media arrived.

  • Radio: the first paid radio commercial aired on WEAF in New York in 1922, and in 1933 Procter & Gamble’s Oxydol began sponsoring the daytime drama Ma Perkins, which is why the genre is called soap opera.
  • Television: the first legal TV commercial ran on July 1, 1941, a ten-second spot for Bulova watches before a Brooklyn Dodgers game that cost the company nine dollars.

Broadcast gave brands a voice, a jingle and a slot in the family’s evening.

It also made brand building expensive, which pushed companies to manage it seriously.

1931: the invention of brand management

On May 13, 1931, a young advertising manager at Procter & Gamble named Neil McElroy typed a three-page memo that changed how companies are organized.

McElroy worked on Camay soap, which was struggling in the shadow of P&G’s own Ivory.

He proposed that every brand should have its own dedicated team led by a brand man who was responsible for everything about it: tracking sales, studying its customers, fixing weak markets and directing its advertising and packaging.

Each brand would be run as its own business and would compete even with its siblings, aimed at a different group of buyers.

P&G adopted the system, and within a generation it was standard across consumer-goods companies worldwide.

McElroy became president of P&G in 1948 and later US Secretary of Defense.

His memo matters because it turned the brand from a label into an organizing principle for a company, and it planted the idea of audience segmentation that positioning would build on forty years later.

The corporate identity era (1907–1980)

Packaged goods taught products to be brands; the next step was to treat the whole company as one.

The prototype came from Germany.

In 1907 the electrical giant AEG hired the architect Peter Behrens as artistic adviser, and he designed its logo, typeface, advertising, products and even its turbine factory as one coherent whole.

Behrens is widely regarded as the first corporate identity designer, and Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier all passed through his office.

After the Second World War, booming corporations merged, diversified and went multinational, and they needed to look like one company everywhere.

The term corporate identity is usually credited to J. Gordon Lippincott of the consultancy Lippincott & Margulies, and a generation of designers gave the discipline its look.

  • Paul Rand: IBM (1956, with the striped version in 1972), Westinghouse (1960), UPS (1961) and ABC (1962).
  • Saul Bass: Continental Airlines (1968), the Bell System (1969), United Airlines (1974) and the AT&T globe (1983).
  • Chermayeff & Geismar: the Chase octagon (1961), one of the first abstract marks for a major American company, and Mobil (1964).
  • Walter Landor: founded his San Francisco firm in 1941 and became the leading name in packaging and consumer brand identity.
  • Massimo Vignelli and Unimark: American Airlines (1967) and the New York City subway signage system.
  • Otl Aicher: Lufthansa (1962–63) and the 1972 Munich Olympics.

I profile several of them in my list of famous graphic designers.

Their lasting invention was the manual as much as the logo.

The Lufthansa manual (1963), the British Rail Corporate Identity Manual (1965), the New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual (1970) and the NASA Graphics Standards Manual (1976) specified how every sign, vehicle, form and uniform should look.

That is the origin of today’s brand guidelines, and the principle has not changed: consistency is what turns a logo into an identity.

A line attributed to Landor sums up the shift in thinking: “Products are made in the factory, but brands are created in the mind.”

Brand image, the USP and positioning (1955–1981)

By the 1950s factories could match each other’s quality, so competing products were functionally the same.

Advertising’s answer was to move the difference out of the product and into the customer’s head.

  • 1955, brand image: Burleigh Gardner and Sidney Levy’s Harvard Business Review article The Product and the Brand argued that people buy the set of feelings and ideas around a product, and David Ogilvy told the advertising industry the same year that every ad is a long-term investment in the image of the brand.
  • 1954–55, repositioning: Leo Burnett took Marlboro, launched in 1924 as a women’s cigarette with the line Mild as May, and relaunched it with a cowboy. The product barely changed; the meaning did, and it became the best-selling cigarette in the world.
  • 1959, the creative revolution: Doyle Dane Bernbach’s Think Small campaign for Volkswagen sold a small, odd-looking car with honesty and wit, and proved a brand could win by having a point of view.
  • 1961, the USP: Rosser Reeves’s Reality in Advertising said every campaign needs a unique selling proposition, one specific benefit that competitors cannot or do not claim.
  • 1969–1981, positioning: Al Ries and Jack Trout argued in a 1969 trade article, a 1972 Advertising Age series and their 1981 book Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind that a brand must own a single idea in the prospect’s mind, relative to its competitors.

Avis is the textbook case: stuck at number two in car rental, it turned that weakness into We Try Harder in 1962.

Positioning is still the core of the strategy work I do before any design starts, and I explain the method in my guide to brand positioning.

Brand equity: brands on the balance sheet (1988–1993)

In the 1980s finance caught up with what marketers had been saying.

1988 was the turning point.

  • Philip Morris bought Kraft for about $13 billion, several times the value of its factories and inventory.
  • Nestlé bought Rowntree, the maker of KitKat, for £2.55 billion, more than double its market value before the bidding started.
  • Rank Hovis McDougall, a British food group fighting off a hostile takeover, worked with the consultancy Interbrand to value its own brands and put £678 million of them on its balance sheet, the first brand valuation of its kind.

The premium that buyers were paying had a name now: brand equity.

David Aaker’s Managing Brand Equity (1991) broke it into awareness, perceived quality, associations and loyalty, and Kevin Lane Keller’s customer-based brand equity model followed in 1993.

Then came a scare.

On April 2, 1993, remembered as Marlboro Friday, Philip Morris cut the price of Marlboro by about 20 percent to fight cheap generic cigarettes.

Its shares fell 23 percent in a day, wiping out roughly $10 billion, other consumer-goods stocks fell with them, and commentators announced the death of the brand.

They were wrong, and the way they were wrong is instructive: the brands that thrived afterwards sold meaning, and the ones that suffered were selling a commodity at a premium.

The numbers since have settled the argument.

Ocean Tomo’s long-running study of the S&P 500 found that intangible assets such as brands, patents and software made up 17 percent of company value in 1975 and about 92 percent in 2025.

Interbrand has ranked the world’s most valuable brands every year since 2000, and its 2025 table puts Apple first at $470.9 billion.

Kantar’s BrandZ ranking, which uses a different method, values its 2026 leader, Google, at nearly $1.5 trillion.

Lifestyle and emotional branding (1980s–2000s)

The brands that came out of the 1990s strongest had stopped talking about their products.

  • Nike: the swoosh cost $35 from design student Carolyn Davidson in 1971, and Just Do It (1988, Wieden+Kennedy) sold determination rather than shoes.
  • Apple: the 1984 Super Bowl commercial directed by Ridley Scott never showed the computer, and Think Different (1997) celebrated rebels instead of specifications.
  • Absolut: a vodka with no heritage became a collectible art series through one bottle-shaped print campaign that ran for about 25 years and some 1,500 ads.
  • MTV: the 1981 logo by Manhattan Design deliberately had no fixed colors, proof that an identity could be flexible and still recognizable.
  • Starbucks: borrowed the sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s idea of the third place between home and work, and sold that, with coffee as the ticket.
  • Intel Inside (1991): made a component nobody sees into a consumer brand, and Walter Werzowa’s five-note chime (1994) became one of the best-known pieces of sonic branding.

I break down how several of these marks changed over time in logo evolution of famous brands.

The ideas spread beyond companies.

Tom Peters’s 1997 Fast Company cover story The Brand Called You launched personal branding, and cities, countries and universities started hiring brand consultants.

The backlash arrived on schedule.

Naomi Klein’s No Logo, published in December 1999, argued that corporations had become brand owners first and producers second, outsourcing manufacturing to sweatshops while they sold image.

The criticism stuck, and it is the root of today’s expectation that a brand’s behavior has to match its story.

Theory caught up in the early 2000s with Marc Gobé’s Emotional Branding (2001), Marty Neumeier’s The Brand Gap (2003) and Kevin Roberts’s Lovemarks (2004), and frameworks such as brand archetypes gave strategists a vocabulary for personality.

The digital era: brands lose control (1994–2019)

The internet handed the microphone to the audience.

The first banner ads appeared on HotWired on October 27, 1994; the best remembered is an AT&T banner that asked whether you had ever clicked your mouse right here, and a reported 44 percent of the people who saw it did.

For a decade the web was mostly a new place to put ads.

Then Facebook (2004), YouTube (2005), Twitter (2006), the iPhone (2007) and Instagram (2010) made every customer a publisher, and a brand became what people say, share and screenshot.

  • Tropicana, 2009: a packaging redesign dropped the orange with a straw; unit sales fell 20 percent in under two months and the old carton came back.
  • Gap, 2010: a new logo was withdrawn after one week of online revolt.
  • Old Spice, 2010: answered fans with 186 personalized videos and doubled sales within months.
  • Oreo, 2013: tweeted You Can Still Dunk in the Dark minutes into the Super Bowl blackout and showed what real-time branding looks like.

I collect more of both kinds in best rebrands and worst rebrands.

Screens changed design too.

Logos had to work as a 16-pixel favicon and an app icon, so identities went flat, simple and responsive, and motion and sound joined the toolkit: Netflix’s ta-dum (2015), Mastercard’s sonic logo (2019), and the craft I discussed with Karsten Kjems in a podcast episode on sonic branding.

A new kind of company appeared that was almost nothing but brand.

Direct-to-consumer startups such as Warby Parker (2010), Dollar Shave Club (2012) and Glossier (2014) owned no stores and often no factories, and competed with incumbents on identity, tone of voice and community.

They also looked alike, and by 2018 fashion houses from Saint Laurent to Burberry had swapped distinctive wordmarks for near-identical bold sans serifs.

The designers Thierry Brunfaut and Tom Greenwood gave the trend a name in Fast Company: blanding.

Meanwhile brand purpose went mainstream: Dove’s Real Beauty (2004), Patagonia’s Don’t Buy This Jacket ad (2011) and Nike’s Colin Kaepernick campaign (2018) showed that taking a position could build a brand, and that a position without proof gets called out within hours.

Branding today: communities, creators and AI (2020–2026)

Four things define the current chapter.

Distinctiveness is back

After a decade of sameness, brands are reaching back into their archives.

Burberry restored its equestrian knight and a serif wordmark in 2023, Pepsi revived the bold look of its 1990s logo the same year, and heritage has become a competitive weapon.

Audiences hold a veto

Customers now act as co-owners who will block a change they dislike.

  • Twitter to X (July 2023): one of the most recognized names on the internet, and a verb, were retired overnight; analysts put the lost brand value in the billions.
  • HBO Max to Max and back (2023–2025): the HBO name was dropped in May 2023 and restored in July 2025.
  • Jaguar (November 2024): a teaser film with no cars in it started a global argument before the product existed.
  • Cracker Barrel (August 2025): removed the old-timer from its logo, lost about $94 million in market value in a day and reversed the change within a week.

People have taken the tools back

Debbie Millman, who has taught the history of branding for years, made a point on my podcast that has stayed with me.

For most of history, symbols were created by people to signal belief and belonging; corporations borrowed that power for a century and a half, and now people are taking it back.

Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter and Me Too have names, marks, colors and slogans, and none of them has a marketing department.

Branding is no longer only a way to sell a different product; it is a way to organize people around an idea.

Her TED talk tells the whole story in fifteen minutes.

Creators are the new consumer brands

People with audiences now launch products the way manufacturers once bought audiences.

MrBeast’s Feastables and Logan Paul and KSI’s Prime both launched in January 2022, and Prime reportedly passed a billion dollars in sales in its second year, because the trust was built before the product existed.

It is the shopkeeper model again: people buy from a person they feel they know.

AI makes assets cheap and distinctiveness expensive

Image generators arrived in 2022, ChatGPT followed that November, and within a year anyone could produce a passable name, logo and website in an afternoon.

Coca-Cola opened its archive to AI artists in 2023 with Create Real Magic, then drew criticism for AI-generated Christmas ads in 2024 and again in 2025, which is the audience veto at work once more.

I use these tools daily, and I have tested most of them in my guide to AI branding tools.

My view is that they repeat the pattern of every earlier technology in this story.

Printing, packaging, broadcast and the web each made it cheaper to produce brand assets, and each time the value moved to whoever had the clearest idea and the most consistent execution.

When everyone can generate a competent logo, a competent logo is worth nothing, and a distinctive, well-positioned one is worth more.

There is also a new audience to brand for: AI assistants that summarize, compare and recommend on a buyer’s behalf, and they reward brands that tell one clear, consistent story everywhere.

What 4,000 years of branding teach us

Here is the pattern I promised at the start: six jobs, added one at a time.

  1. Claim: whose is this? (livestock brands, seals)
  2. Vouch: who made it, and can I trust it? (makers’ marks, hallmarks)
  3. Protect: who may use this mark? (trademarks)
  4. Persuade: why this one and not the one next to it? (advertising, the USP, positioning)
  5. Express: what does choosing it say about me? (corporate identity, lifestyle and emotional branding)
  6. Connect: what is it like to deal with them, and what do other people say? (digital, social, community)

A brand today has to do all six at once.

When I build an identity, I check that the name can be owned and registered, that the mark signals who stands behind the work, that the positioning gives buyers a reason to choose, that the design carries the right meaning, and that the whole system holds up in the places where customers talk back.

A few practical lessons fall out of the history.

  • Keep the promise. The hallmark worked because the silver really was tested; design cannot rescue a promise the business does not keep.
  • Be distinctive. The Bass triangle, the Coca-Cola script and the contour bottle lasted because they looked like nothing else, and blanding showed what happens when everyone follows the same trend. Jenni Romaniuk of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute put it simply when we talked about distinctive brand assets: if lots of competitors use red, red is not a smart choice.
  • Stay consistent. The identity manuals of the 1960s and 70s made modest logos feel monumental through repetition.
  • Own one idea. Volvo and safety, Avis and effort, Nike and determination; positioning is as useful for a ten-person firm as it was for them.
  • Change carefully. Tropicana, Gap and the reversals of the 2020s show that recognition is an asset customers feel they own, so audit what people recognize before you redraw it (my brand refresh guide covers how).
  • Expect technology to lower the cost of assets and raise the value of ideas. It was true of the printing press and it is true of AI.

History of branding: FAQ

When did branding start?

Branding started more than 4,000 years ago: Indus Valley merchants were sealing trade goods with carved marks by about 2600 BCE, and Egyptian tomb art shows cattle being branded with hot irons.

Commercial branding in the modern sense, with registered trademarks, packaging and advertising, dates from the second half of the 1800s.

Who invented branding?

No single person invented branding, because marking goods arose independently in Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, China and Rome.

The people most often credited with inventing modern branding are Josiah Wedgwood, who built a named, premium pottery brand in the 1760s and 70s, and Neil McElroy, whose 1931 Procter & Gamble memo created brand management.

What is the oldest brand in the world?

It depends on the definition.

The Roman lamp maker FORTIS is among the oldest known commercial brand names, Beretta has documented sales from 1526, and the Bass pale ale label (1876) is the UK’s first registered trademark and is still in force.

Twinings says it has used the same wordmark since 1787, which is widely cited as the oldest logo in continuous use, and Lyle’s Golden Syrup holds the Guinness World Record for the oldest branding on packaging, dating to 1885.

What was the first registered trademark?

The Bass & Co. pale ale label, with its red triangle, became UK trade mark number 1 when the British register opened on January 1, 1876.

France had a registration law from 1857, and in the United States the first federal registration went to the Averill Chemical Paint Company in October 1870.

Why is it called branding?

It is called branding because the word brand originally meant fire or a burning piece of wood, and to brand was to burn a permanent mark into livestock, timber or casks.

The word moved from the mark on the barrel to the goods inside it by 1854, and then to the reputation behind the goods.

What is the difference between a brand and branding?

A brand is the perception people have of a company, product or person, while branding is the work done to shape that perception through strategy, naming, design, messaging and behavior.

You own your branding; your audience owns your brand.

How has branding changed over time?

Branding has moved from marking ownership, to guaranteeing origin and quality, to legally protected trademarks, to persuasion through advertising, to identity and emotional meaning, and finally to a two-way relationship shaped by customers online.

Each stage added to the previous ones rather than replacing them.

Why is the history of branding important?

The history of branding matters because it shows which principles survive every change of technology: keep the promise, be distinctive, stay consistent and own one clear idea.

Those principles are as useful to a startup choosing its first logo as they were to a Roman lamp maker.

Build a brand that lasts

The brands that survive for centuries have a clear promise, a distinctive mark and the discipline to stay consistent, and none of that requires a big-company budget.
